title: Can't build Flutter Applications on old x86_64 CPUs with 3.16.0 and greater
body: I upgraded from Flutter 3.10 to Flutter 3.16.3, and I am now on stable 3.16.4 with Dart 3.2.3 on Windows 10. Creating a new sample project exits with code 3221225501, often just after printing “Downloading package sky_engine...”. Running the project for Windows fails through MSBuild with MSB8066 and exits with -1073741795. Removing the project's windows folder, running flutter clean, and cleaning or repairing the Dart pub cache have not changed it. What is causing this exit code, and how can I build projects successfully again?

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from Flutter 3.10 to the 3.16 line, flutter create exits with code 3221225501, often immediately after “Downloading package sky_engine...”.
A Windows build ends with MSB8066 and exit code -1073741795.
The same errors remain after flutter clean, pub-cache cleaning or repair, and removing the project's windows folder.
N0.label: N0 Flutter tool exits unexpectedly

symptoms_visible: Flutter 3.16 still exits with code 3221225501 after I try the suggested MSB8066 troubleshooting and reinstall the SDK.
N1_x.label: N1_x generic Windows build troubleshooting aftermath

symptoms_visible: New projects work with Flutter 3.10.5, 3.13.0, and 3.13.9, but Flutter 3.16.0 and 3.16.4 stop or fail on Android, Windows, and web.
My affected computer has an old x86_64 processor, although it meets Flutter's documented Windows system requirements.
N1.label: N1 version boundary and old CPU established

symptoms_visible: The Flutter command continues to terminate on the affected old x86_64 machines when tested at bad revisions during the bisection.
N2.label: N2 raw regression bisections collected

symptoms_visible: Running a tiny Dart program that evaluates 42.0.floor() crashes with -1073741795 on the affected machine, while the same command with --target-unknown-cpu prints 42.
The CPU trace says “sse41? no” and the ordinary run then crashes.
N3.label: N3 Dart CPU-dependent crash isolated

symptoms_visible: After updating to a stable Flutter build containing the Dart fix, I can build and run the project on Windows and web, and the ceil test prints 1016 without crashing.
N_terminal.label: terminal fixed build verified by affected users

solution.intent: Treat the failure as a generic Windows MSB8066 or damaged Flutter installation problem and retry standard project cleanup, Visual Studio troubleshooting, or SDK reinstallation.
solution.concrete_example: Try the standard MSB8066 suggestions, reinstall Flutter, recreate the Windows project files, and clean the build and pub caches.

edges.comment: Messages c0-c3 on the reporter's system: the reporter had already tried the linked MSB8066 suggestions, then reinstalled and tested multiple Flutter SDK versions. The latest versions continued to fail, so generic Windows-build cleanup was falsified.

question_patterns: Which Flutter versions work and which versions show the failure?
Can you compare a new project on an older Flutter SDK with the current SDK?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried new projects with 3.10.5, 3.13.0, 3.13.9, 3.16.0, and 3.16.4. The first three worked, but 3.16.0 and 3.16.4 would not build properly.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every version, including 3.10.5 and 3.13.9, fails in exactly the same way.
3.13.9 is the last working version, while both tested 3.16 patch versions fail.

question_patterns: What processor does the affected computer use?
Is there anything unusual or particularly old about the affected hardware?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: This is a very old x86_64 system. My machine uses an AMD Phenom II X4 965; other affected machines use an AMD Athlon II, AMD Phenom II, or Intel Core 2 Quad.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It also reproduces on a current-generation x86_64 CPU with SSE4.1 support.
The affected machine has 16 GB of RAM instead of 8 GB.

question_patterns: Does this computer meet Flutter's documented Windows system requirements?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I checked the linked requirements, and my device meets the documented system requirements.

question_patterns: Can you create a new project and run flutter run -v on Android, Windows, and web?
Does the failure affect only the Windows target, or do verbose runs fail on other targets too?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I created a new project and ran the verbose commands. With the affected Flutter version it fails on Android, Windows, and web; it is not limited to the Windows CMake project.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Android and web work normally; only the Windows desktop build reaches MSB8066.

edges.comment: Messages c3-c13 and c9: the original reporter supplied the version matrix, AMD Phenom II CPU, requirements check, and multi-platform verbose runs. Other affected users supplied compatible old-CPU examples; they are explicitly folded into the simulated user side.

question_patterns: After those troubleshooting attempts, which Flutter versions still work on this computer?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Flutter 3.10.5, 3.13.0, and 3.13.9 work here. New projects on 3.16.0 and 3.16.4 still fail.

question_patterns: What CPU is in the affected system?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My affected system has an old AMD Phenom II X4 965. Other people seeing the same failure have similarly old AMD or Intel x86_64 processors.

question_patterns: Have you checked the published Windows system requirements?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, and this system meets the requirements listed there.

question_patterns: Please run a fresh project verbosely on Android, Windows, and web and report which targets fail.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The fresh project fails with the affected SDK on Android, Windows, and web, so the symptom is not confined to MSBuild.

edges.comment: Recovery from the failed generic-troubleshooting branch using the reporter's c3-c9 evidence and the old-CPU reports in c12-c13. No participant's unrelated setup is used as a separate causal problem.

question_patterns: Can you git bisect the Flutter repository between a working revision and a failing revision and paste the final output?
Please continue the Flutter SDK bisection until git prints the first bad commit.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On one affected machine, git printed “47ba59c762919d66811b72acab9732d6aa2a93c9 is the first bad commit,” an engine roll dated July 12, 2023. A separate affected machine printed “ee4208fd26abd5c91680b4aa185df0ae9e00ce61 is the first bad commit,” another engine roll dated July 13, 2023.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The bisection lands on a project-template-only change with no engine or Dart roll nearby.
Repeated runs still land on adjacent engine rolls from the same two-day window, but disagree about which roll is first bad.

edges.comment: Messages c37-c45: participant9 and participant7 ran the requested bisections on their own affected old-CPU machines. Their raw outputs disagree on the exact first bad Flutter commit, so the answer preserves both outputs and does not claim that either user identified the underlying Dart change.

question_patterns: Using Dart from the affected Flutter installation, can you run a program containing main() { print(42.0.floor()); } normally and again with --target-unknown-cpu?
What raw output do you get from the small floor.dart probe with and without the alternate CPU target flag?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Running dart floor.dart produces a crash dump with ExceptionCode -1073741795. Running dart --target-unknown-cpu floor.dart on the same machine prints 42.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both commands print 42 and neither Dart process crashes.
The ordinary command crashes with the same exception code, while the alternate-target command prints 42 using Dart 3.3 rather than Dart 3.2.

question_patterns: Can you run the provided diagnostic Dart executable with --trace-cpuid and paste its output?
Please paste the processor lines from that diagnostic run and say what happens immediately afterward.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The trace prints my old CPU identification and says “sse41? no sse2? yes”. After that, the normal execution crashes with -1073741795. We obtained the same “sse41? no” result on old AMD and Intel machines.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The trace says “sse41? yes” and the same tiny program still crashes at the same point.
The processor brand differs, but the trace still reports SSE2 present, SSE4.1 absent, followed by the same crash.

edges.comment: Messages c47-c61 and c70: affected users ran the handler-requested floor.dart and CPUID probes on their own machines. Their answers contain only raw command output. Another affected user independently reported that WinDbg stopped on roundsd; that unprompted observation is recorded in N3.volunteered_info. The Dart VM interpretation remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Use a current stable Flutter SDK containing the Dart VM fix for JIT CPU-feature restrictions on old x86_64 processors, then verify project creation and builds on the affected machine instead of relying on cleanup or permanent downgrades.
solution.concrete_example: The Dart VM was recognizing that these CPUs lacked SSE4.1 but was not applying that restriction everywhere during JIT compilation, allowing an unsupported instruction such as roundsd to be generated while the Flutter tool ran. The fix was reviewed in Dart and shipped with Flutter 3.19.5 using Dart 3.3.3. Update to that or a newer stable build, create a fresh project, and retest Windows and web before closing the issue.
solution.inference_hint: The users established that normal Dart JIT execution crashes, the conservative CPU-target mode succeeds, and CPUID reports no SSE4.1. The Dart maintainer concluded that CPU detection itself worked but a hole in applying the resulting restrictions allowed unsupported instructions during JIT compilation. Mapping the crash to that VM mechanism is engineer inference, not an answer the reporter supplied.

edges.comment: Messages c63-c78 establish the accepted diagnosis, Dart review, and stable hotfix. Messages c80-c86 provide terminal-side verification from participant7 and participant9 on their own affected old-CPU systems; these affected users are folded into the simulated user side. The original reporter did not personally post the final retest, so the confirmation is not attributed solely to that person.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the Dart VM's JIT CPU-feature restrictions were not applied everywhere, allowing an SSE4.1 instruction such as roundsd to execute on old x86_64 CPUs that report no SSE4.1 support.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: older Flutter versions work, the affected machines use old CPUs, normal floor.dart execution crashes, the conservative CPU-target run prints 42, and the CPUID trace reports no SSE4.1.

Must recommend updating to a stable Flutter build containing the Dart VM fix rather than treating SDK reinstallation, cache cleanup, MSB8066 troubleshooting, mixed path separators, or a permanent downgrade as the resolution.
Must ask an affected user to verify project creation and Windows or web builds on the updated SDK before declaring the issue resolved.
Resolution requires an affected old-CPU user to report successful builds on a build containing the fix; the thread supplies that verification through affected participants folded into the user side.

persona_hint.experience_level: The original reporter is a capable Flutter user who can switch SDK versions, run verbose commands, inspect system requirements, and follow Git checkout instructions. Additional affected users folded into the user side can run git bisect, standalone Dart diagnostics, CPUID tracing, and test fixed builds.
persona_hint.communication_style: Polite, patient, and evidence-oriented. Provides command output when asked, clearly distinguishes working and failing versions, and asks for concrete diagnostic steps when unsure.
